messages.subject: recursion blues
parts:
This is my first post, so please forgive me if you have already discussed this as a group previously.

I'm struggling with make a recursively solving a set of equations.  I'm 1) looking to see if anyone knows a good way to do this, and 2) wondering if anyone can help me un-mangle the for loops I'm attempting to do this with.  So here's what I'm trying to do:

I have two equations that I need to simultaneously solve for a single unknown: P.  Here are the 2 equations:


where m is mass (both initial 0, and at time=t), P is production rate, k is a rate constant, t is time, n is isotope spike mass (both initial 0 and at time=t), and alpha is an isotope factor that stays constant (here it's 0.98). I know everything in both of these equations except P.

Ultimately, I'm trying to get the best estimate for a biological rate (P=production rate).  Soooo, I need to recursively solve for predictive values of m(at time=t) and n(at time=t), and then find the value for P that minimizes the combined least-square errors when comparing the measured values of m and n with their predicted values (predicted using estimates for P).  The error equation (which takes into account variation in both m and n variables):

where APobserved(t) is the isotope Atom Percent (measured) at time=t, APexpected(t) is the predicted atom percent at time=t, SDobs-AP is the standard deviation of all AP values throughout the experiment, Nap is a normalization factor for atom percent, mobserved(t) is the mass measured at time=t, mexpected(t) is the predicted mass at time=t, SDobs-m is the standard deviation of all mass values throughout the experiment, and Nm is a normalization factor for mass.

Then I can just sort the data to find the smallest Error value, and then I'll know my optimal P! 

The bugger comes with creating a recursive function that combines all 3 of these equations, and spits out the proper matrix of sort-able results.
My data structure: There are 72 incubation jars. Each jar was measured for AP (atom percent observed), n (isotope spike mass) and m (total mass) a total of 5 times, at hours 24, 336, 480, 720 and 960.  Values for k (the rate constant) and a predicted n (n at time=t) were calculated.

Here's my worded version of code needed:
calculate StDev for AP (ap_sd_obs) and Mass (mass_sd_obs) for all data together throughout the incubation
calculate StDev for AP (ap_sd_prec) and Mass (mass_sd_prec) for all instrument standards (given by SIF)
calculate normalization factors for AP (nap) and mass (nmass) for all data together with the following equations:
#nap <- (ap_sd_obs/ap_sd_prec)
#nmass <- (mass_sd_obs/mass_sd_prec)

make a list of a range of possible P values #make this span from -10,000 to +10,000
make an empty matrix to receive output #dimensions of 8 columns (jar, timepoint, n_pred, P, mt, nt, E)  x 100,000 rows (5 timepoints/jar * number of estimates of P)
solve mt equation
#mt = (P/k)-((P/k)-mi)^(-k*t))
solve nt equation
#nt = ((ni^(-k*a*t))/((P/k)-((P/k)-mi)^(-k*t))*mt
output sets of values for mt and nt
#so for each estimate of P, both equations are solved and should return 5 sets of mt and nt values for each new P estimate
#(i.e. mt1, mt2, mt3, mt4 and mt5; nt1, nt2, nt3, nt4 and nt5 at t = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 for each P value)
calculate LSE estimate using error equation (comparing predicted mt and nt values to the measured values for each time step)
#E = (((|n_measured - nt|)/ap_sd_obs)*nap) + (((|m_measured - mt|)/mass_sd_obs)*nmass)
Find the P value with the smallest estimated Error value

##########################

#Full-disclosure: I'm awful at for loops, which is the only way I can think of to do this recursive fitting stuff, so forgive my clumsy code, please, but here are my attempts
P <- c(-10000:10000)
jar <- data$jar[1:72]
t <- c("24","336","480","720","960")
k <- data$k[1:72]
m <- data$m
n <- data$n
mi <- data$m[1:72] #because the "initial" mass value is the first mass at the first timepoint
ni <- data$n[1:72] #because the "initial" spike mass is the spike mass for the first timepoint

foo <- function(data, jar, P, t, k, mi, m, ni, n){
  results <- c(jar=1, t=2, P=3, m_pred=4, n_pred=5)
  results.frame <- matrix(ncol=5, nrow=(P*5))
  for (i in 1:72){
    for (j in 1:5) {
      m_pred[i,j] <-(P/k)-(((P/k)-mi)^(-k*t))
      n_pred[i,j] <- ((ni^(-k*a*t))/((P/k)-mi)^(-k*t))*m
      results <- data.frame()
    }
  }
}

Another version, trying to use 'foreach' loops (which theoretically make output matrix-building automatic...?)

foo2 <-
  foreach(b=t, .combine='cbind') %:%
  foreach(a=P, .combine='c') %do% {
  foo(P, t) #or make a function that is nested for loops like above but without the output matrix specifications...
   }
foo2
#add in another foreach loop to handle the output of the E term??

############################################

Okay, that's enough rambling for me.  I've attached my .csv file, so you can see what I'm working with.  If you have any thoughts, either about this code and making it better (aka:work), or of another/better way to do this type of recursive fitting function, please hit me back.  Thanks so much in advance!

-Kim

You're a goddess!  This is so close, but I have two lingering issues, about which I'm properly stumped.

1) The 'out' matrix is populated with calculated values for  mt, nt, and lse, but the columns for lse_min and p are "NA" which is no good, because those are the two columns (aka: values) that I care about:

...etc.

This is the code:

data <- read.csv("recursion2.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",")

data$sdo_ap <- rep(0,72)
for (i in 1:72) {

data$sdo_ap[i] <- sd(data$ap[which(data$jar==i)])}
data$sdo_m <- rep(0,72)
for (i in 1:72) {

data$sdo_m[i] <- sd(data$m[which(data$jar==i)])}
data$sdo_ap <- rep(data$sdo_ap[1:72], 5) #populate the whole column
data$sdo_m <- rep(data$sdo_m[1:72], 5) #populate the whole column

sd_prec_ap <- 0.000356894591861632 #from SIF
sd_prec_m <- 28 #this is based on my FAOMx stdev of standards (spreadsheet:"GC_master.xlsx") b/c SIF didn't give

data$nap <- (data$sdo_ap/sd_prec_ap)
data$nm <- (data$sdo_m/sd_prec_m)

data$k <- abs(data$k) #everything messes up when this isn't positive!

data$mi <- rep(data$m[1:72], 5)
data$ni <- rep(data$n[1:72], 5)
data$ape <- ((data$n/data$m)+0.0105) #calculating the APexpected(t) needed for LSE

out <- data.frame(jar=data$jar, t=data$t)

#need starting values outside the range of possibility
out$lse_min <- 10000
out$p <- 1000000

for (i in -10000:10000){

out$mt <- (i/data$k)-(((i/data$k)-data$mi)^(-data$k*data$t))
 
  out$nt = ((data$ni^(-data$k*data$ap*data$t))/((i/data$k)-((i/data$k)-data$mi)^(-data$k*data$t)))*out$mt
 
  out$lse <- ((((abs(data$ap-data$ape))/data$sdo_ap)*data$nap)
              + (((abs(data$m-out$mt))/data$sdo_m)*data$nm))
out$lse_min <- ifelse(out$lse < out$lse_min, out$lse, out$lse_min)

out$p <- ifelse(out$lse == out$lse_min, i, out$p)
}

############################

2) Another peculiarity that I've noticed when trying to run this with different ranges of P: when you restrict the range to smaller values, the LSE estimates are much smaller...  This shouldn't be the case.  The larger ranges still include the values used in the smaller range, so using a larger range should only be able to decrease the lowest LSE estimate.  That makes, sense, right??

parts:
#1 is happening because some of your calculations are generating NAs (probably because p is unrealistic in some cases? - you should really investigate this to make sure it's kosher and not an error in the formulas). Once an NA is generated, the ifelse() comparisons at the bottom of the loop fail and you are no longer keeping proper track of the lowest lse.

To fix it, add this line directly below the out$lse calculation in the -10000:10000 for loop:

out$lse <- ifelse(is.na(out$lse), 100000000, out$lse) #if out$lse is NA, set it to 100000000 so it doesn't cause out$lse_min to take an NA value


If you run head(out, 50) after fixing your code, you'll see that some of the lse_min values are still 10,000 which means 10,000 is too small an initial value. I set it to 100000000 instead and that appears to behave correctly now.

As for #2, the out$lse, out$mt, and out$nt fields are just the output of the most recent calculation. if you want out$mt, out$nt, and out$lse calculated for the minimums, you need to do one final set of calculations after the loop with out$p as the value for p


Also: I think you need to be careful here, because when I run your code after I made the change in #1 described above, all the outputted values of p are 0, 1, or 3. I don't know what the expected behavior of these formulas is but this seems like an awfully narrow set of results given the range of potential values for p.

The full code, including fixes, is below, with changes in bold:
-----

data <- read.csv("recursion2.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",")

data$sdo_ap <- rep(0,72)

for (i in 1:72) {
data$sdo_ap[i] <- sd(data$ap[which(data$jar==i)])}
data$sdo_m <- rep(0,72)

for (i in 1:72) {
data$sdo_m[i] <- sd(data$m[which(data$jar==i)])}
data$sdo_ap <- rep(data$sdo_ap[1:72], 5) #populate the whole column
data$sdo_m <- rep(data$sdo_m[1:72], 5) #populate the whole column

sd_prec_ap <- 0.000356894591861632 #from SIF
sd_prec_m <- 28 #this is based on my FAOMx stdev of standards (spreadsheet:"GC_master.xlsx") b/c SIF didn't give

data$nap <- (data$sdo_ap/sd_prec_ap)
data$nm <- (data$sdo_m/sd_prec_m)

data$k <- abs(data$k) #everything messes up when this isn't positive!

data$mi <- rep(data$m[1:72], 5)
data$ni <- rep(data$n[1:72], 5)
data$ape <- ((data$n/data$m)+0.0105) #calculating the APexpected(t) needed for LSE


out <- data.frame(jar=data$jar, t=data$t)

#need starting values outside the range of possibility
out$lse_min <- 100000000

out$p <- 1000000

for (i in -10000:10000){
out$mt <- (i/data$k)-(((i/data$k)-data$mi)^(-data$k*data$t))

out$nt = ((data$ni^(-data$k*data$ap*data$t))/((i/data$k)-((i/data$k)-data$mi)^(-data$k*data$t)))*out$mt

out$lse <- ((((abs(data$ap-data$ape))/data$sdo_ap)*data$nap)
+ (((abs(data$m-out$mt))/data$sdo_m)*data$nm))
out$lse <- ifelse(is.na(out$lse), 100000000, out$lse)

out$lse_min <- ifelse(out$lse < out$lse_min, out$lse, out$lse_min)
out$p <- ifelse(out$lse == out$lse_min, i, out$p)
}
